newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt dominant in minor metals, eyes Zaire, DLA.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt dominant in minor metals, eyes Zaire, DLA.

text.p: Cobalt was again in the spotlight in the minor industrial metals market during the past week as traders mulled the situation in Zaire and Wednesday's U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) sale. Elsewhere, chrome flew higher on the wings of increased demand from the aerospace industry while, despite news that Chinese producers were trying to hold prices around $2,300 a tonne, antimony held little changed levels.
Although the chaos in Zaire was far removed from the mining belts of the Shaba region traders voiced strong concern over the situation which showed few signs of easing.
One suggested intesified fighting between government troops and rebels over the last week had the potential to possibly spread to the mining region.
"If anything the fighting is likely to spread rather than die down," one European trader said.
Zaire produces between 4,000/5,000 tonnes of cobalt in total per year. Currently the market is extremely short of material.
"If Zaire is taken out of the equation the market will suffer in terms of supply and demand," one trader said.

Elsewhere, in the cobalt arena talk reverberated over the DLA sale. "Its been a magor talking point," one trader said. On Wednesday, the DLA said it sold a total of 200,806 lbs of cobalt for an average $19.47/lb. Glencore Ltd of Stamford Conn was the sole successful recipient, the DLA said.
The DLA received bids on Monday for a total of 999,537 lbs of contained cobalt but, it said, several bidders failed to comply with terms and conditions and were ineligible for awards.
Metal Resources Group Ltd, also known as Minor Metals Incorporated (MMI), expressed disappointment over the U.S. Defence Logistics Agency (DLA) cobalt tender award.
"We note that out of four grades of cobalt being tendered the DLA awarded material against only the two lowest grades," MMI said in a statement.
"Despite bidding for a total of 488,418 lbs cobalt MMI was not successful and awards were made for a total of 200,806 lbs cobalt to another party."

"We are disappointed that the DLA awarded 54,492 lbs of 99.05 percent cobalt at $19.01 a lb to a party and declined MMI's bid for the same item at $19.78 a lb due to a technicality," it said. One European merchant believed that the long term strategy of the recipient of the metal was bolstered by the sale.
"The material was of good quality and helps them (Glencore) to meet long term objectives," the trader said. "They seem willing and committed to meet their consumer demands," the merchant added.

But several traders were somewhat surprised that the all the cobalt was awarded to Glencore. They were under the impression following the recent Cobalt Development Institute (CDI) meeting held in Pittsburgh that the award would be made on a pro rata basis. This would have then meant that other higher bidders should have been awarded material in preference to Glencore.
They were also surprised the DLA only awarded such a small quantity.
The overall view of the sale was seen as bullish as nearly all the offered metal was bid for.
Several market operators had assumed that around 453 tonnes of cobalt would hit the market. In the event only around 91 tonnes will be released.
Traders said the next sealed bid for DLA cobalt is not scheduled until March 1997 and they also noted talk that the French stockpile of the metal was exhausted.

Chrome shone, against the backdrop of low available material and flew higher. Traders said one major Chinese producer had no available stocks to hand. They also noted that Russian metal was also at low levels.
Despite a move by Chinese antimony producers to hold prices around $2,300 a tonne FOB the market was unmoved from its recent solid price range around $2,000/$2,150, warehouse Rotterdam.

Elsewhere the other minor metals held around unchanged levels. Germanium is unlikely to spark any consumer interest until 1997, a trader said. Indium dipped as consumers refused to enter the market and buy. They were banking on near-term lower prices.
